questions.enonce_markdown:
In the "scattering of alpha particles experiment", the results obtained by Geiger and Marsden can be summarized by the diagram below;

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2025-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

(i) Give the mass number of an alpha particle?

(ii) Explain why a few of the alpha particles were deflected at large angles?

(iii) Explain why most of the alpha particles went through undeflected? *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, $^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{2+}$ (2 protons + 2 neutrons): its **mass number is 4**.

**(ii) Large-angle deflections.** The atom contains a very small, very dense, **positively charged nucleus** which holds almost all of the mass. An alpha particle (positively charged) that comes very close to a nucleus is **strongly repelled by the electrostatic force** between like charges, and is deflected through a large angle (a very few are even turned back). Deflection by a nucleus needs a close approach, which is rare.

**(iii) Undeflected particles.** The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom (about $10^{-5}$ times its diameter): **most of the atom is empty space**, in which only the very light electrons move. The great majority of the alpha particles therefore pass through the gold foil without coming near a nucleus, and the electrons are far too light to deflect the heavy, fast alpha particles.

questions.enonce_markdown: The half-life of tritium, a radioactive isotope of hydrogen is 12.25 years. Beginning with a 2.5 g sample of tritium, what mass will be left after 45 years? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Number of half-lives $n = \dfrac{45}{12.25} = 3.67$.

Mass remaining $m = m_0 \left(\dfrac12\right)^{n} = 2.5 \times \left(\dfrac12\right)^{3.67} = 2.5 \times 0.0784 \approx 0.196\ \mathrm{g}$.

**About 0.20 g of tritium remains** (0.196 g).

Equivalent form: $m = m_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{12.25} = 0.0566\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}$, giving $2.5\,e^{-0.0566\times45} = 0.196\ \mathrm{g}$. (Check by halving: after 3 half-lives, 36.75 y, $2.5/8 = 0.3125$ g; after 4 half-lives, 49 y, $0.156$ g; 45 y lies between, so 0.196 g is reasonable.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Collision Theory of Reaction Kinetics was developed from the kinetic theory of gases.

(i) State two postulates of the Collision Theory.

(ii) Hydrogen peroxide decomposes according to the equation:

$\mathrm{2H_2O_2(aq) \rightarrow 2H_2O(l) + O_2(g)}$.

State and explain one method by which the rate of the reaction can be measured

(iii) Given that the rate law for the reaction is $\mathrm{Rate = K[H_2O_2]^2}$. What does K represent *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two postulates of the collision theory** (any two):

1. A reaction can occur only when the reactant particles (molecules, atoms or ions) **collide** with one another; the rate depends on the frequency of collisions.
2. Only **effective collisions** lead to reaction: the colliding particles must have a combined kinetic energy **equal to or greater than the activation energy, $E_a$**.
3. The colliding particles must also be in the **correct orientation** at the moment of collision.

**(ii) Method for measuring the rate.** *Collect the oxygen gas.* Place the hydrogen peroxide solution (with the catalyst, e.g. $\mathrm{MnO_2}$) in a flask connected to a gas syringe (or an inverted measuring cylinder or burette over water), start a stopwatch, and read the **volume of $\mathrm{O_2}$ every 30 s**. Plot volume against time: the **gradient of the tangent** to the curve at a given time is the rate of reaction at that time (rate $= dV/dt$), the initial gradient being the initial rate. This works because oxygen is the only gas formed, so the volume of $\mathrm{O_2}$ is proportional to the amount of $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ that has decomposed.

(Alternative: withdraw samples at intervals, quench them in ice-cold water and titrate the remaining $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ with acidified $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$, then plot $[\mathrm{H_2O_2}]$ against time.)

**(iii) K** is the **rate constant** of the reaction: the proportionality constant in the rate equation, numerically equal to the rate when $[\mathrm{H_2O_2}] = 1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$. It is constant for a given reaction at a given temperature (it increases with temperature, following the Arrhenius equation) and is independent of concentration. For the printed second-order law its units are $\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

| Bond type | Species involved | Example of compound with the type of bond |
|---|---|---|
| Ionic bond | Positive ions (cations, usually from a metal) and negative ions (anions, from a non-metal), held by electrostatic attraction after **transfer of electrons** | $\mathrm{NaCl}$ (also $\mathrm{MgO}$, $\mathrm{CaF_2}$) |

| Dative covalent bond | A **donor** atom with a lone pair of electrons and an **acceptor** with an empty orbital: the shared pair comes entirely from the donor | $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ (also $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$, $\mathrm{H_3N{\rightarrow}BF_3}$, $\mathrm{Al_2Cl_6}$) |

questions.enonce_markdown: Suggest an explanation for the trigonal pyramidal shape of $\mathrm{NH_3}$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown: The nitrogen atom of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ has **four electron pairs** in its outer shell: **three bonding pairs** (N-H) and **one lone pair**. By the valence-shell electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory the four pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible, in a **tetrahedral** arrangement. Only three of the four positions are occupied by atoms, so the molecule has a **trigonal pyramidal** shape. The lone pair repels more strongly than a bonding pair (lone pair-bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair-bond pair repulsion), which squeezes the H-N-H angle to about $107^{\circ}$, slightly less than the tetrahedral angle $109.5^{\circ}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two pure liquids A and B, have vapour pressures of $1.5 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ and $3.5 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ respectively at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. If a mixture of the two liquids is prepared by adding 2.5 moles of A and 1.5 moles of B at the same temperature, calculate:

(i) The partial vapour pressure of A and B in the mixture:

(ii) The total vapour pressure of the mixture. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Assume an ideal solution, so that **Raoult's law** applies: $p_i = x_i\,p_i^{\circ}$.

Total moles $= 2.5 + 1.5 = 4.0$. Mole fractions: $x_A = \dfrac{2.5}{4.0} = 0.625$ and $x_B = \dfrac{1.5}{4.0} = 0.375$.

**(i) Partial vapour pressures**

$p_A = 0.625 \times 1.5\times10^{4} = 9.375\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (about $9.4\times10^{3}$)

$p_B = 0.375 \times 3.5\times10^{4} = 1.3125\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (about $1.3\times10^{4}$)

**(ii) Total vapour pressure** (Dalton's law): $P = p_A + p_B = 9.375\times10^{3} + 1.3125\times10^{4} = \mathbf{2.25\times10^{4}\ N\,m^{-2}}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A solution made up of $0.15\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ propanoic acid ($\mathrm{K_a} = 1.35\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$) and $0.35\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ sodium propanoate, constitutes a buffer solution.

(i) What is a buffer solution?

(ii) Calculate the pH of the solution. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A **buffer solution** is a solution that **resists changes in pH** when small amounts of acid or base are added (or when it is diluted). An acidic buffer contains a **weak acid and its salt** (its conjugate base), here propanoic acid and sodium propanoate.

**(ii) pH.** The salt is fully ionised, so $[\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COO^-}] \approx [\text{salt}] = 0.35$ and $[\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}] \approx [\text{acid}] = 0.15\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ (the weak acid is barely ionised).

$$K_a = \frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} \Rightarrow [\mathrm{H^+}] = 1.35\times10^{-5}\times\frac{0.15}{0.35} = 5.79\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$$

$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}(5.79\times10^{-6}) = \mathbf{5.24}$

(Check with Henderson-Hasselbalch: $\mathrm{p}K_a = 4.87$; $\mathrm{pH} = 4.87 + \log(0.35/0.15) = 4.87 + 0.37 = 5.24$.)
